paragraphs.heading: Five belts around the globe
paragraphs.text: On the basis of latitude, the globe is divided into three broad heat zones: torrid, temperate and frigid. The temperate and frigid zones each exist once in the north and once in the south. The Torrid Zone covers 39.78% of Earth's surface, from the Tropic of Cancer at latitude 23°26′08.9″ N to the Tropic of Capricorn at latitude 23°26′08.9″ S. Each temperate zone runs from its tropic to the Arctic or Antarctic Circle at 66°33′51.1″ and covers 25.99%. Each frigid zone runs from that circle to the pole at 90° and covers 4.12%.

paragraphs.heading: The Torrid Zone
paragraphs.text: The Torrid Zone is also known as the tropics. Its northern and southern boundaries mark the farthest latitudes at which the Sun passes directly overhead. On those two lines this happens once a year, while inside the tropics the Sun is overhead twice in a year. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer at the June solstice and at the Tropic of Capricorn at the December solstice, and it returns to the equator for the March equinox.

paragraphs.heading: The temperate zones
paragraphs.text: In the two temperate zones the Sun is never directly overhead. The climate there is mild and generally ranges from warm to cool, and these latitudes include subtropical areas. Four seasons occur here each year: spring, summer, autumn and winter.

paragraphs.heading: The frigid zones
paragraphs.text: The two frigid zones, or polar regions, are Earth's coldest regions, and ice and snow generally cover them. The Sun's rays always arrive at a slant, so they give less heat per horizontal surface area. For part of the year these zones experience the midnight sun and the polar night. At the edge of the zone, the Sun is too low to rise on one day, the winter solstice, and on one day at the summer solstice it stays above the horizon for 24 hours. At the pole, the day is one year long: half of it daylight and half of it night.

paragraphs.heading: An idea from ancient Greece
paragraphs.text: Parmenides, a scholar of ancient Greece, first put the concept forward, and Aristotle modified it in a lasting way. Both divided the Earth into three types of climatic zones according to distance from the equator. Thinking, like Parmenides, that the area near the equator was too hot to live in, Aristotle gave the name Torrid Zone to the region around the equator, between 23.5° N and 23.5° S. Both reasoned that the region from the Arctic Circle to the pole was permanently frozen. It was thought uninhabitable and was named the Frigid Zone. That left the northern Temperate Zone, lying between the other two, as the one area believed to be habitable.

paragraphs.heading: What held up, and maps today
paragraphs.text: In fact, people have lived in almost every climate on Earth, the inside of the Arctic Circle included. As geography became better known, a second temperate zone was found south of the equator, and a second frigid zone around the Antarctic. Aristotle's map was oversimplified, but the general idea was correct. The climate map most commonly used today is the Köppen climate classification, which the climatologist Wladimir Köppen (1846–1940) developed. It splits the world into five major climate regions using three measures: average precipitation over the year, average precipitation by month and average temperature by month.
